analysis.one_liner: Strips states of their power to police securities fraud by major public companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Thomas MacArthur with 5 Republican cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar any state law, rule, or enforcement action from regulating securities fraud for companies listed on major national exchanges like the NYSE and Nasdaq. All civil securities fraud lawsuits would have to be filed in federal court, not state court. States could keep going after fraud in smaller, non-listed securities, and could still bring criminal cases—but only if those followed federal standards. The practical effect is to replace states' own fraud rules (often stricter, like New York's) with the federal government's single standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies and their executives, who would face only one federal anti-fraud standard instead of stricter or overlapping state rules, and would be shielded from state regulators bringing their own fraud actions.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any state law, rule, or enforcement action from regulating securities fraud with respect to an issuer of covered securities, meaning companies listed on the NYSE, Nasdaq, or similar exchanges.
Gives federal district courts exclusive jurisdiction over civil securities fraud actions and lets companies move any state-court case to federal court.
The bill's stated findings argue that differing state 'blue sky' rules raise compliance costs, create reputational risk for accused companies, and provide no material investor protection benefit.
States keep authority only over securities that are not covered securities, and any state criminal enforcement of fraud in covered securities must comply fully with federal legal requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Investors and the state securities regulators that police markets for them. When a listed company misleads investors, state regulators like state securities commissions would no longer be able to bring their own civil fraud actions under their own, sometimes tougher, standards. Any fraud claims over major listed companies would have to run through federal court under federal standards alone.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges the trade-off by design: it eliminates concurrent federal and state jurisdiction over covered companies, so state-level tools for policing securities fraud—tools some states have used more aggressively than federal regulators—would be removed.

The CRS summary confirms the bill generally limits state regulation of securities fraud and establishes exclusive federal jurisdiction over civil securities fraud actions, meaning investors lose a venue and a set of legal standards.

The bill would preserve state civil enforcement only for non-covered securities, so most large public companies—the kind whose securities ordinary people hold through retirement accounts—would be exempt from state fraud oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefit is uniformity: companies operating in every state today face multiple overlapping state fraud statutes, and the bill's findings argue this raises costs without adding investor protection. The cost is that state enforcers—sometimes quicker and tougher than the SEC, and able to act under broader standards like New York's—would be barred from policing the largest companies. Weighing those honestly, the bill trades away a layer of fraud enforcement that ordinary investors rely on in exchange for lower compliance costs for public companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas MacArthur introduced the bill on February 15, 2018, joined by Reps. Davidson, Tenney, and McHenry.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; that was its only action.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies benefit from the bill's failure only in the sense that nothing changed—but the outcome preserved the status quo, in which state regulators can still pursue securities fraud by major companies under their own laws. Investors and state securities regulators kept their existing protections.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and no chamber ever considered it.

industries.note: Listed companies would be subject only to federal anti-fraud standards, escaping state regulators and state-court suits. Their gain comes directly out of the enforcement tools investors and state regulators use to hold them accountable for misleading investors.

State securities commissions would lose the power to bring civil fraud actions over covered securities under their own laws, including broader statutes like New York's Martin Act. Their enforcement role for the largest companies would be eliminated.

Exclusive federal jurisdiction would move all civil securities fraud cases to federal court, where procedural hurdles like the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act make suits harder and restrict plaintiffs' choice of venue.
